makingABudget.title: How to Make a Budget — With Tether-Zero and Your AI Coach in Your Corner

intro.p1: If you've ever reached the end of the month wondering where your paycheck went, you're not alone — and the fix is simpler than you might think. A budget is just a written plan for your money. It helps you make sure you have enough every month, keeps you from running out before the next paycheck, and gives you a way to save for goals and emergencies.
intro.p2: The steps below follow the classic budgeting process recommended by the Federal Trade Commission's consumer.gov. Along the way, we'll show how Tether-Zero handles the mechanics for you — and how Zero, your built-in AI coach, acts like a financial mentor who's already read your numbers and knows exactly where you are in the process.

whatIsABudget.heading: What Is a Budget?
whatIsABudget.p1: A budget is a plan that shows two things: how much money you make, and how you spend it. When you see those numbers side by side, patterns jump out — categories where you can spend less, areas where you'd rather spend more, and savings opportunities hiding in plain sight.
whatIsABudget.p2: Tether-Zero is built on a specific flavor of this idea called zero-based budgeting: every dollar you earn gets a job before the month begins. Your Budget board tracks this with the To Be Budgeted indicator — yellow when money is still unassigned, red if you've allocated more than you earn, and green when you hit exactly zero.
whatIsABudget.p3: New to zero-based budgeting? This is Zero's first job. Instead of sending you off to read tutorials, you can simply ask — “What does To Be Budgeted mean?” or “Why is my indicator red?” — and get an answer grounded in your budget, not a generic explainer. You can even pick the coaching style that keeps you motivated: the encouraging Cheerleader, the no-nonsense Drill Sergeant, or the data-driven Analyst.

gettingReady.heading: Getting Ready
gettingReady.p1: The traditional first step is gathering bills, pay stubs, and bank statements so you're working from real numbers instead of guesses.
gettingReady.p2: In Tether-Zero, this step mostly disappears. Connect your bank through Plaid sync and your accounts and transactions flow in automatically. Prefer to stay hands-on? Manual accounts, manual entry, and transaction import are fully supported too.
gettingReady.p3: Where Zero helps: With your transaction history connected, Zero can see your actual spending patterns from day one. Ask “What do I typically spend on groceries?” and you'll get an answer based on your real history — the honest starting numbers most first-time budgeters never have.

step1.heading: Step 1: List Your Bills and Expenses
step1.p1: Write down everything you spend money on: fixed bills like rent and utilities, plus variable expenses like groceries, gas, and entertainment.
step1.p2: In Tether-Zero, this list becomes your Category Groups and Categories — organize spending into groups like Needs, Wants, and Savings, with categories underneath. Sinking Funds handle irregular expenses (car repairs, holiday gifts, annual insurance) by rolling unspent balances forward month to month, and Smart Match auto-categorization learns your patterns and files incoming transactions for you.
step1.p3: Where Zero helps: Not sure how to structure your categories, or whether an expense belongs in a sinking fund? Ask. “Should my car insurance be a sinking fund or a regular category?” gets a practical answer with the reasoning behind it — the kind of judgment call that usually stalls new budgeters for a week.

step2.heading: Step 2: Figure Out Your Monthly Income
step2.p1: Total up what you bring in each month — paychecks plus anything else regular, like child support.
step2.p2: Tether-Zero gives income its own Income group at the top of your Budget board, with Planned and Received columns, so you can watch actual deposits fill in against your plan. If your income varies, the classic advice is to average your last twelve months — and with your history synced, that's a question Zero can answer for you rather than a spreadsheet exercise.
step2.p3: Where Zero helps: Zero also watches for income you didn't plan on. The Windfall Interceptor notices when a deposit lands well above your normal paycheck — a tax refund, a bonus — and prompts you before it quietly disappears into everyday spending: apply it to your top debt, and Zero tells you exactly how much interest you'd save and how many days sooner you'd be debt-free.

step3.heading: Step 3: Subtract Expenses From Income
step3.p1: Here's the core math: income minus bills and expenses. The result should be more than zero. If it's negative, you're spending more than you make.
step3.p2: The To Be Budgeted indicator computes this live as you allocate. And because zero-based budgeting asks you to assign every dollar, Tether-Zero flips the goal: deliberately allocate any surplus to savings or debt until you reach exactly zero.
step3.p3: Where Zero helps: This step is where budgets get emotionally hard — cutting back means choosing. Zero turns vague guilt into concrete trade-offs. Ask “Can I afford this $300 purchase?” and the Opportunity Cost Simulator answers with the actual consequence: “Technically yes, but it pushes your debt-free date back a week.” If you carry debt, Zero's Strategy Auditor goes further, watching your APRs and balances and telling you when switching between Debt Crusher's Snowball and Avalanche strategies would save you real money — with the Freedom Horizon chart showing the payoff date move as you decide.

step4.heading: Step 4: Use Your Budget Every Month
step4.intro: A budget isn't a document you make once — it's a monthly routine:
step4.li1: Beginning of the month: Make your plan. Copy Budget pulls last month's allocations forward in one click, and Zero can help you adjust it based on what actually happened last month.
step4.li2: Throughout the month: With Plaid sync and Smart Match, tracking mostly happens automatically — your job shrinks to a quick review.
step4.li3: Watch for problems early: This is where Zero earns its keep. Beyond the standard overspend alerts, Zero's predictive pacing alerts catch problems before they happen: if half your dining budget is gone by the 5th, Zero warns you that you're projected to run dry by mid-month and suggests a daily spend that gets you to the 31st. You course-correct on day 5, not day 31.
step4.li4: End of the month: The budget summary panel ranks your most overspent and underspent categories, and Zero can walk you through what the numbers mean for next month's plan.
step4.partner: Budgeting with a partner? Tether-Zero Households support shared budgets with role-based access — and Zero plays neutral third party. Instead of one partner accusing the other, Zero surfaces the data dispassionately: “Shopping is trending 20% higher than last month — want to look at the transactions together?” It also celebrates joint milestones, because crossing into positive net worth together deserves more than a spreadsheet cell turning green.

savings.heading: Make Savings Part of the Plan
savings.p1: The FTC's advice is to treat savings as one of your budgeted expenses rather than whatever happens to be left over — and zero-based budgeting bakes this in. Create financial goals in Tether-Zero with a target amount and date, and the app calculates the required monthly contribution and tracks your pacing. Ask Zero “How much do I need to set aside monthly to have $3,000 by June?” and you'll get the number plus a read on whether your current budget can absorb it.

finalThoughts.heading: Final Thoughts
finalThoughts.p1: Making a budget takes one sitting: list what you spend, total what you earn, and give every dollar a job. Keeping a budget takes a few minutes a day — less when bank sync, auto-categorization, and alerts do the bookkeeping.
finalThoughts.p2: What's historically been missing from budgeting apps is the coach: someone to answer “is this normal?”, “can I afford it?”, and “what should I do next?” in the moment, with your actual numbers in hand. That's Zero. It doesn't wait for you to dig through a help menu — it shows up contextually, right when a windfall lands, a category runs hot, or a strategy stops being optimal. The fundamentals of budgeting haven't changed since the FTC wrote them down. What's changed is that you no longer have to work them out alone.

whyBudgetsFail.heading: Why most first budgets fail before they start
whyBudgetsFail.p1: Traditional budget templates drop you into about 35 ready-made categories, most of which have nothing to do with your life. If you don't own a car, why is there a category for oil changes? Before you've budgeted a single dollar, you're doing chores — deleting, renaming, second-guessing.
whyBudgetsFail.p2: There's a quieter problem too: entering your debts into a cold, clinical form can feel like being graded. Plenty of people abandon setup right there. Tether-Zero's wizard was designed to remove both failure points — it only creates what matches your answers, and it talks about debt the way a friend would.

fiveQuestions.heading: Five quick questions about your real life
fiveQuestions.p1: The wizard opens with “Let's build your budget” and asks you to name your household. Then it gets personal, in the best way: “Where do you live?” Renting, paying a mortgage, owned outright, or living with family — plus which utilities you pay. Each answer quietly becomes a budget category you would otherwise have created by hand.
fiveQuestions.p2: “How do you get around?” covers personal vehicle, public transit, rideshare, or bike and walking — with quick toggles for a car payment and car insurance. The wizard pays attention: mention a car payment here, and the debts step arrives with an auto loan already selected, marked “Added from your earlier answer — deselect if it doesn't apply.”

Nothing feels mandatory: every step after housing has a “Skip this step” link, and if life interrupts you mid-setup, the wizard saves your progress and greets you next time with “Pick up where you left off?”

noJudgment.heading: The step with no judgment
noJudgment.p1: Between transportation and lifestyle comes the question most apps fumble: “What are you working to pay off?” The screen says the rest in Tether-Zero's own words: “This is what we're here to crush — no judgment.” Credit cards, student loans, personal loans, auto loans, medical debt — or simply “No debt.”
noJudgment.p2: The wording is deliberate. Debt in Tether-Zero is something you crush — it's the same spirit behind the Debt Crusher payoff planner — and crushing it starts here, by giving every debt payment a home in your budget from day one instead of treating it like a confession.

review.heading: Review everything, then “Create my budget”
review.p1: Nothing is created behind your back. The review step lays out exactly which budget groups and categories your answers produced, organized and expandable, so you can look before you commit. Something off? Step back, change an answer, and the preview updates. The budget only becomes real when you tap “Create my budget.”
review.p2: The result is typically a budget of 12–20 categories that actually match your life — not 35 you'll spend an evening pruning. A few essentials are always included, like Groceries and an Emergency Fund, and as the wizard itself puts it: “You can add, rename, or remove anything later.”

firstTenMinutes.heading: Your first ten minutes of actual budgeting

Work down your categories in priority order — essentials first, then debt payments, then everything else — until the To Be Budgeted amount at the top reads $0. It turns green when you get there. That's zero-based budgeting: every dollar has an assignment.
firstTenMinutes.p2: If you run out of money before you run out of categories, that isn't failure — it's the most honest financial information you've had in a while. Fund what matters most; the rest waits for your next paycheck.

envelopeBudgeting.title: Give Every Dollar a Job: Envelope Budgeting with Monthly Allocations

intro.p1: Long before budgeting apps, people did this with cash and paper envelopes: payday came, the money got divided — rent in this envelope, groceries in that one — and when an envelope was empty, the spending stopped. It worked because it made one decision unavoidable: every dollar got a job before it got spent.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero is built on that same principle, minus the paper cuts. Each month you allocate your income across your budget categories until your income minus your allocations equals exactly zero — what the app calls balance to zero. This guide walks through how monthly allocations work, and how the app handles the arithmetic, the remembering, and the honest-mirror part for you.

envelopeMethod.heading: The envelope method, minus the envelopes
envelopeMethod.p1: In Tether-Zero, your categories are the envelopes. Every category row in your budget shows two numbers: Allocated — what you put in the envelope this month — and Available — what's still in it after spending. Fill them at the start of the month or whenever you're paid, spend against them, and glance at Available before any purchase you're unsure about.
envelopeMethod.p2: The Available number does the bookkeeping a paper envelope did physically: it's whatever you allocated, plus anything carried in from before, minus what you've spent. When it's healthy, spend without guilt. When it's low, that's the envelope telling you it's nearly empty — not a judgment, just arithmetic.

tbb.heading: To Be Budgeted: the number that tells the truth
tbb.p1: Above your categories sits To Be Budgeted — the money you have that hasn't been given a job yet. In the app's own words: “Green means you've hit balance to zero, yellow means money is still waiting, and red means you have assigned more than you have.”
tbb.p2: A positive number is unemployed dollars — money without a job tends to get spent by accident, so assign it, even if its job is simply next month's bills. A negative number means you've promised money you don't have; pull back from your lowest-priority categories until you're at zero. And zero is a floor for honesty, not a ceiling for savings — giving every dollar a job includes the dollars headed for goals and savings.

guidedSetup.heading: Let Guided Setup do the math
guidedSetup.p1: Facing a fresh month and a column of empty envelopes, you'll see a banner offering help with that month's budget: “Set each category one at a time — income first, with the math done for you.” Tap Start Guided Setup and the wizard does exactly that.
guidedSetup.p2: Its opening screen is titled, fittingly, Balance to Zero. Every answer saves immediately, so you can stop at any point and pick up right where you left off — and the To Be Budgeted chip updates as you go, so you watch yourself budget your way from yellow to green.

sinkingFunds.heading: Envelopes that remember: sinking funds
sinkingFunds.p1: Some expenses don't arrive monthly — car repairs, holiday gifts, annual insurance premiums. For those, mark a category as a Sinking Fund: unspent funds automatically roll over to the next month instead of resetting, so the envelope quietly grows until the bill shows up.
sinkingFunds.p2: Say your Car Repair fund carried $200 in from previous months and you allocate another $100 this month: Available shows $300, ready for the day the check-engine light wins. That's the difference between an emergency and an inconvenience.

newMonth.heading: A new month in one click
newMonth.p1: Once you've dialed in a month you like, you never start from scratch again: Copy Budget brings all of another month's allocations into the new one in a single click, and you adjust from there. Budgeting month two takes minutes, not an evening.
newMonth.p2: And when a category goes over — one will, and that's fine — Tether-Zero flags it plainly as overspent, you move money from a category that can spare it, and the month goes on. Do that consistently and the app even tracks your streak of consecutive weeks with no overspent categories. Overspending handled honestly isn't failure; it's the system working.

startSmall.heading: Start smaller than you think
startSmall.p1: The envelope method fails when there are too many envelopes. Ten categories you actually check beat forty you abandon — you can always split “Food” into “Groceries” and “Dining Out” later, once your real patterns show up. Your first month's allocations will be guesses; by month three they'll be facts.

sinkingFunds.title: Stop Getting Ambushed by “Surprise” Expenses: Sinking Funds Explained

intro.p1: Every budget has a villain story that goes the same way: the month was going fine, and then the car registration came due, or the vet found something, or December happened. The budget “blew up.” But look closer and most of these ambushes share a secret — they were never surprises at all. They were scheduled.
intro.p2: These are irregular certainties: expenses that don't arrive monthly but absolutely arrive. A sinking fund is the old, unglamorous, extremely effective fix — set aside a little every month so the money is already waiting when the bill lands. Tether-Zero builds them into the budget itself. Here's how to use them.

onSchedule.heading: Surprises that arrive on schedule
onSchedule.p1: Car registration comes once a year, every year. Tires wear out every few years, reliably. December brings gifts every single time. None of this is an emergency — yet these irregular certainties wreck more budgets than any restaurant habit ever did, because a monthly budget quietly assumes every month looks the same.
onSchedule.p2: It helps to keep two buckets straight. An emergency fund is for the genuinely unknown — the job loss, the broken arm. Sinking funds are for the known-but-irregular: you can name the expense, roughly when it's coming, and roughly what it costs. Different problems, different envelopes.

math.heading: The math that makes big bills small
math.p1: The trick is one division. Take a $600 insurance premium due in twelve months: that's a budget-breaking lump, or it's $50 a month and a non-event. Divide what the expense costs by the months until it arrives, and that's your monthly amount.
math.p2: Stack a few of these — $50 for the premium, $50 toward holiday gifts, $40 toward tires, $50 for a vet-visit buffer — and about $190 a month quietly disarms four future ambushes at once. The expenses didn't change; the schedule did.

flipSwitch.heading: Flip one switch in Tether-Zero
flipSwitch.p1: In Tether-Zero, a sinking fund is an ordinary budget category with one switch flipped. When you create or edit a category, enable Sinking Fund — the dialog explains it in one line: “Unspent funds will automatically roll over to next month.” Allocate to it like any other category, and on the 1st of each month the leftover balance carries forward automatically.
flipSwitch.p2: Set aside $100 a month for car insurance and don't touch it, and six months later the category shows $600 available. The fund's tooltip breaks the balance down — Allocated, Balance Forward, Spent, Available — so you always know how much is this month's money versus what's been quietly accumulating.

honest.heading: Honest even when you overspend
honest.p1: What if the bill arrives before the fund is ready? Say you've budgeted $200 for car repairs and the actual repair costs $230. The fund doesn't reset and pretend nothing happened — the $30 shortfall carries forward as a negative balance, so next month's $200 allocation shows $170 actually available.
honest.p2: That sounds strict, but it's the kindest thing a budget can do: show you the true number. A deficit that carries forward gets noticed and fixed with one extra allocation; a deficit that silently vanishes gets repeated.

fundOrGoal.heading: Sinking fund or goal?
fundOrGoal.p1: Tether-Zero also has Financial Goals, and the line between the two is worth knowing. A good rule of thumb: recurring cycles — insurance, holidays, car maintenance — work best as plain sinking funds. One-time targets with an amount and a date — a $2,000 vacation next August — shine as goals, which add a target amount, a pacing indicator that tells you whether you're on track, and progress visuals.
fundOrGoal.p2: If in doubt, start with the sinking fund. You can always create a goal later, once the thing you're saving for has a specific finish line.

spendIt.heading: Spend it — that's the point
spendIt.p1: When the expense finally arrives, spend from the fund like any other category. The balance drops — possibly to zero — and that's not a setback: it's the money doing exactly the job you hired it for, while the rest of your monthly budget never feels a thing. And if a fund outlives its purpose, Tether-Zero lets you release the category's available funds back to your budget.
spendIt.p2: Start smaller than you think: scan the last twelve months of statements for everything that made you say “where did that come from?”, then pick two or three funds — not ten. Fully funding car maintenance and holidays beats sprinkling $10 across eight envelopes. For how sinking funds fit into the bigger monthly rhythm, see our guide to <link>envelope budgeting with monthly allocations</link>.

irregularPaycheck.title: Budgeting on an Irregular Paycheck: Pay Cadence and Holding Categories

intro.p1: Nearly every piece of budgeting advice starts with the same quiet assumption: one predictable paycheck, arriving once a month, always the same size. If that's not your life — you freelance, you drive gigs, you earn commission, or you're simply paid every two weeks — the standard advice wobbles right where you need it most.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero handles the irregular on purpose, with two tools that work together: pay-frequency math that converts what you earn into what a month actually delivers, and the holding category — a buffer that lets you budget from money you have rather than money you're expecting. Here's how they work.

monthlyLie.heading: The monthly-budget lie
monthlyLie.p1: Zero-based budgeting has one weak spot: it quietly assumes a predictable paycheck. When income is variable, that assumption pushes you into allocating money you merely expect — and when a client pays late or a slow month hits, every envelope you funded on a projection turns out to be partly fiction.
monthlyLie.p2: The fix isn't different math; it's a different order of operations. Budget from reality, not projections: money gets a job only after it lands. Everything below exists to make that ordering easy instead of heroic.

realMoney.heading: Budget the money that actually lands
realMoney.p1: Start with the income side. Your budget's Paychecks category comes with pointed advice built in: enter take-home, not gross — Tether-Zero budgets the dollars that actually land in your account. Withholding, taxes, and platform fees never reach your budget, so they don't belong in it.
realMoney.p2: And when you run the Guided Setup, income comes first, before any spending category — so every allocation that follows is drawn against a number grounded in what your account will really see.

cadenceMath.heading: Math for every pay cadence
cadenceMath.p1: When the Guided Setup reaches your income it also asks, “How often does this happen?” — weekly, every two weeks, monthly, or yearly — and then does the calendar arithmetic for you. Bring home $800 every two weeks, and the wizard shows the conversion plainly: $800 × 2 paydays this month = $1,600. You budget what this month actually delivers.
cadenceMath.p2: The same math catches the happy surprises. Twice a year, a biweekly schedule produces a third payday, and the wizard calls it out — “August has 3 paydays — that's an extra $800 you can put toward debt or savings.” It works in the other direction for annual bills too: a yearly amount is divided by twelve so the money is already waiting by the due month — the same idea behind <link>sinking funds</link>.

holdingBuffer.heading: A buffer for lumpy income
holdingBuffer.p1: Now the freelancer's half. Create a category — “Client Payments Buffer,” say — and flip on Holding Category. The dialog is blunt about what it does: “Funds held here are excluded from spending totals.” When an invoice finally pays, the money goes here first: earned, held, not yet promised to anything.
holdingBuffer.p2: Your budget header then tells the whole truth in three numbers. Income $5,000, Allocated $3,200, Total Holding $1,200 — leaving $600 To Be Budgeted. Committed money, buffered money, and undecided money stay visibly separate, which is exactly the visibility a variable income demands.

releaseFunds.heading: Release funds when the money is real
releaseFunds.p1: When you're confident the cash is truly yours to spend, open Release Holding Funds and move an amount from the buffer into a spending category — $500 from the buffer to Groceries in one atomic step, both sides updating together. Tether-Zero won't let you release more than the buffer actually holds.
releaseFunds.p2: Holding categories are also excluded from your overspent and underspent analytics, so managing your buffer never pollutes your spending insights. And they're deliberately not sinking funds — a category can be one or the other, never both. A sinking fund is a savings bucket that grows month over month; a holding category is a staging area for this month's incoming cash.

rhythm.heading: A rhythm for the irregular
rhythm.p1: Put together, a payday routine emerges: when a check lands, park it in the holding category. Release enough to fund the bills due before the next check, then debt payments, then groceries and gas. As more income confirms, release more. Your envelopes only ever contain real dollars, so spending from them requires no faith.
rhythm.p2: And in the months when the calendar gifts you a third payday, you'll already know where the extra goes. Irregular income doesn't disqualify you from budgeting — it's the strongest reason to keep a budget that tells the truth.

catchOverspendingEarly.title: Catch Overspending Before It Happens: Pacing Alerts and the Pacing Gauge

intro.p1: There's a particular sinking feeling that shows up around the 28th of the month: you open the budget, and a category you thought was fine is deep in the red. The money is already gone, so there's nothing left to decide — just a hole to patch. A budget that only tells you what already happened isn't really a plan; it's a post-mortem.
intro.p2: The fix isn't more willpower — it's earlier information. Tether-Zero watches the pace of your spending all month long and speaks up while a problem is still small. Here's how the Spending Pace gauge and Zero's pacing alerts work together to help you stop overspending before it happens, not explain it afterward.

whySneaks.heading: Why overspending sneaks up on you
whySneaks.p1: Nobody decides to blow the grocery budget. It happens $23 at a time, and every trip looks reasonable on its own. The trouble is that a budget total only tells you where you stand against the whole month — not whether you got there on day 9 or day 26. Having 20% of your dining-out money left is comfortable on the 28th and a real problem on the 12th, and the number alone can't tell you which one you're living.
whySneaks.p2: In a zero-based budget the damage doesn't stay put, either. Every dollar already has a job, so when a category goes negative, covering it means pulling money away from another job — and overspending you don't catch until month-end quietly borrows from next month's plan. Timing, it turns out, is most of the game: the earlier you know your pace is off, the smaller and calmer the fix.

gauge.heading: Your month at a glance: the Spending Pace gauge
gauge.p1: This timing problem is exactly what the Spending Pace gauge on the Insights dashboard solves. One dial compares two numbers: the percentage of your budget you've spent, and the percentage of the month that has elapsed. When they rise together, the gauge reads On Track. Spend a bit faster than the calendar and it shifts to Slightly Ahead; outrun the month entirely and it turns red with Over Budget.
gauge.p2: The dial is deliberately forgiving. The green zone runs to 85% of pace and a yellow band covers the stretch to 100%, so a normal, slightly lumpy month doesn't set off alarms — and Tether-Zero pauses zone warnings in the first days of a new month, when a single grocery run can make the math look scarier than it is. All the gauge asks is that you've set a monthly budget; allocate your categories and it starts reading your pace right away.

alerts.heading: Pacing alerts: a nudge before the damage is done
alerts.p1: The gauge watches your month as a whole; pacing alerts watch every category individually. Zero, your built-in AI coach, compares each category's spending against how much of the month has passed, with a built-in 15% buffer so ordinary unevenness doesn't trigger false alarms. When a category genuinely outruns the calendar, an amber Pacing Warning card appears in Coach's Corner on your dashboard — while there's still month left to act.
alerts.p2: Each warning does the forecasting for you: it names the category, projects the date the money will run out, and estimates the overspend if nothing changes. From there you're one tap from a fix — Adjust budget jumps straight to your budget, and Dismiss clears the card. And it won't nag you: a dismissed warning stays gone unless your spending speeds up even further.

courseCorrect.heading: Pacing fast? Three calm ways to course-correct
courseCorrect.p1: A pacing warning is information, not a verdict. Often the right response is simply to ease off — learning on the 12th that dining out is running hot is exactly what makes the next two weeks fixable. Just as often, the honest answer is that the target was set too low, and the right move is the one the card offers: adjust the budget to match your real life.
courseCorrect.p2: And sometimes the month is just lumpy — you bought a year of dog food in week one. Then the move is the classic envelope fix: <link>move money over from a category with room to spare</link>, and the plan is whole again. Whichever you choose, you're choosing early, while all three options are still on the table. That's the entire point.

habit.heading: Make it a one-minute habit
habit.p1: None of this asks for evening spreadsheet sessions. Glance at the Spending Pace dial when you open Tether-Zero — one look says whether the month needs anything from you at all. Over in your Budget, the Overview panel carries the same idea as Month Pacing — how much you've spent against how much of the month has passed — with any overspent categories visible at a glance.
habit.p2: That's the whole practice: let the gauge watch the month, let Zero watch the categories, and spend your attention only where something actually drifts. If you don't have a budget to pace against yet, <link2>build your first one in about ten minutes</link2> — then let it run. Budgets rarely fail in one dramatic blowout; they fail in small drifts nobody noticed. Now you'll notice.

snowflakePayments.title: The Power of Snowflake Payments: How $20 Here and There Moves Your Debt-Free Date

intro.p1: The debt snowball is famous: pay minimums on everything, throw everything extra at one debt, repeat. But the strategy has a small, overlooked cousin that does outsized work — the snowflake. A snowflake is $20 from selling an old lamp. A $75 rebate. The birthday check from grandma. Money too small to feel strategic, and exactly the money most plans waste.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero's Debt Crusher treats snowflakes as first-class citizens: log one, and the app shows you — in days — how much sooner you'll be debt-free. This guide covers what counts, where the money goes, and why watching the date move is the most motivating thing a budget can do.

whatCounts.heading: What counts as a snowflake
whatCounts.p1: The app defines it right on the page: “A snowflake is any extra, unexpected money you can put toward debt — like tax refunds, bonuses, birthday money, or proceeds from selling items.” The key word is unexpected. Your regular monthly debt payment is already in your plan; a snowflake is found money on top of it.
whatCounts.p2: That's what separates snowflaking from tightening your budget. You're not squeezing groceries to free up $20 — you're catching money that would otherwise evaporate into everyday spending and giving it a one-time job with a permanent payoff.

measurableTime.heading: Small money, measurable time
measurableTime.p1: Here's what makes the feature more than a ledger: instant feedback. Apply a snowflake — say a $500 tax refund — and Tether-Zero recalculates your entire payoff plan on the spot, then answers in the only unit that matters: days. In that example, roughly sixty of them — two months closer to free.
measurableTime.p2: Every snowflake in your history carries its own receipt — “45 days saved” next to one, “12 days saved” next to another. Debt payoff is a long game, and long games are lost to invisibility. A number that moves the same day you act is what keeps you playing.

smartRouting.heading: Routed where it hurts debt most
smartRouting.p1: You don't have to decide where the money goes. Leave the target empty and the app applies it automatically — the helper text says it plainly: “Leave empty to auto-apply to your #1 priority debt.” Which debt that is depends on your active strategy: the smallest balance if you're running Debt snowball, the priciest interest rate on Debt avalanche.
smartRouting.p2: And no snowflake is ever wasted on a technicality. Apply $2,000 against a debt with only $1,500 left, and the first $1,500 finishes that debt while the remaining $500 rolls straight into the next one in line.

freedomHorizon.heading: Watch your Freedom Horizon move
freedomHorizon.p1: The payoff shows up where you'll see it daily. The dashboard's Debt-Free Date tile tracks your projected freedom date, and the Debt Crusher spells out the headline: “You'll be debt-free 14 months sooner than minimum-only payments.” Snowflakes push that number further.
freedomHorizon.p2: The Freedom timeline turns it into a progress bar with a personality — “You're ahead — 6 weeks to go” — so every snowflake you log nudges a status you can feel. Debt payoff stops being an abstraction and starts being a date on the calendar with your name on it.

findingSnowflakes.heading: Where snowflakes come from
findingSnowflakes.p1: Once you start looking, they're everywhere: the tax refund, the quarterly bonus, the side-gig payout, the $40 from decluttering the garage, the rebate you forgot you filed. None of them was in your budget — which is precisely why each one is a snowflake and not a line item.
findingSnowflakes.p2: Paid every two weeks? Twice a year the calendar hands you a whole extra paycheck — Tether-Zero even flags it during budget setup as money you can put toward debt or savings. An entire <link>third payday</link> is the biggest snowflake most households ever get.

Partners with Viewer access can browse the record even though only Editors and Admins can log or remove payments, so the wins are shared and the data stays clean.
keepReceipts.p2: Logged one by mistake? Delete it, and the impact of every remaining snowflake is recalculated so the math never drifts from reality. Honest numbers, visible progress, small money doing big work — that's the whole trick.

payOffDebtFaster.title: Snowball vs. Avalanche: Pick Your Debt Payoff Strategy with a Side-by-Side Simulation

intro.p1: Ask the internet how to pay off debt faster and you'll land in the middle of a decade-old argument. One camp says attack the highest interest rate first, because math. The other says knock out the smallest balance first, because motivation. Both camps have spreadsheets, success stories, and absolute certainty — which doesn't help you much when you just want a plan you can start this month.
intro.p2: Here's the secret the argument buries: both methods work. The real question isn't which strategy is best in the abstract — it's which one gets you debt-free, with your debts, your rates, and your temperament. That's a question you can answer with a simulation instead of a debate, and it's exactly what Tether-Zero's Strategy Simulator was built for.

oneEngine.heading: Every payoff plan is the same engine
oneEngine.p1: Strip away the branding and snowball and avalanche share one chassis. You pay the minimum on every debt, every month — no exceptions; that keeps everything current. Then you take every extra dollar you can spare and aim it at a single focus debt. When that debt dies, its entire payment rolls into the next focus debt, and the payments compound like a boulder gathering speed. The only difference between the two methods is the order of the targets.
oneEngine.p2: In Tether-Zero, the “extra” has a name: your Monthly Debt Budget — the amount your household commits to debt payoff above the minimums. Set it once in Debt Crusher, and every projection you're about to see is built from it. It's the throttle of the whole engine: the strategies decide where the money goes, the Monthly Debt Budget decides how hard it pushes.

avalanche.heading: The avalanche: highest interest first
avalanche.p1: The Avalanche Method orders your focus debts by interest rate, highest first. A 27% credit card gets every spare dollar before a 6% car loan sees a cent beyond the minimum. The logic is pure arithmetic: the highest rate is where your money bleeds fastest, so stopping that bleed first pays the least total interest — and it's usually the fastest route to zero in pure dollar terms.
avalanche.p2: The catch is emotional, not mathematical. If your highest-rate debt is also your biggest balance, you can pour money into it for a year before you get to celebrate closing a single account. Some people are fine running on arithmetic alone. Plenty of us aren't — and a plan you abandon in month seven saves you nothing.

snowball.heading: The snowball: smallest balance first
snowball.p1: The Snowball Method ignores interest rates and orders your debts by balance, smallest first. That $400 store card goes first — not because it's costing you much, but because it can be gone in a month or two. Each cleared debt is a real, visible win: one fewer bill, one fewer creditor, proof the plan is working.
snowball.p2: Yes, it usually costs somewhat more in total interest than the avalanche. What it buys with that money is momentum — and debt payoff is a years-long game where momentum is frequently the scarcest resource. The best strategy on paper is worthless if you quit it, and quick wins keep people in the game.

simulator.heading: Stop guessing: see both futures side by side
simulator.p1: This is where the argument ends and your numbers take over. On the Debt Crusher dashboard, the Strategy Simulator shows the Snowball Method and Avalanche Method side by side — each with your projected Debt Free Date and the months remaining, computed from your actual debts and your Monthly Debt Budget. Sometimes the gap between the two is years; often it's smaller than the internet's shouting suggests. Either way, you're choosing between two real dates, not two philosophies.
simulator.p2: Flip the toggle and the whole plan recalculates instantly — payoff order, focus debt, projections, everything. The simulator asks only two things: at least two debts to compare, and a Monthly Debt Budget so it has a throttle setting to project from. Curious what the comparison feels like before signing up? There's a <link>sample simulator right on our homepage</link> you can play with in ten seconds.

commit.heading: Commit as a household — and switch freely
commit.p1: Debt payoff is a team sport, so your chosen strategy is shared by the whole household: one person flips the toggle and everyone's dashboard reflects the same plan. Partners with view-only access see the strategy and its projections without being able to change them — everybody sees the same Debt Free Date, and nobody can quietly rearrange the plan.
commit.p2: And the choice isn't a tattoo. Start with the snowball for a few quick wins, then switch to the avalanche once the momentum is real — the plan recalculates the moment you do. If you haven't set up your budget yet, <link2>start there</link2>: the Monthly Debt Budget needs a budget around it to be honest. Then pick a date, pick the strategy that gets you there in one piece, and let the boulder roll.

canIAffordThis.title: What Does That Purchase Really Cost? Using the Opportunity Cost Simulator Before You Buy

intro.p1: The jacket says $400, and the checkout page agrees. But if you're paying down debt, the sticker is only the first installment. Every dollar you spend is a dollar that never reaches your balances — and interest keeps running on everything that stays behind. The real price of a purchase includes the extra weeks of payments it quietly signs you up for.
intro.p2: Most of us feel that truth as a vague twinge at checkout. Tether-Zero turns the twinge into a number. Ask Zero, the AI financial coach built into the app, whether you can afford something, and the Opportunity Cost simulator answers with your actual payoff math: how far your Debt Free Date slips and how much extra interest tags along. Not a lecture — a receipt, before you buy.

truePrice.heading: The price tag isn't the whole price
truePrice.p1: Economists call it opportunity cost: the true cost of anything is what you give up to get it. When you're working a payoff plan in Debt Crusher, what you give up is progress. Money that could have shrunk a balance this month stays on the card instead, and the interest meter runs a little longer on every debt behind it. That's why Tether-Zero reports a purchase's true cost as the sticker price plus the additional interest it creates — the number the store never prints.
truePrice.p2: Picture a $500 purchase landing on a card you're actively paying down. Depending on your balances, rates, and monthly debt budget, that one swipe might push your Debt Free Date back about three weeks and add close to $48 in interest — a true cost near $548. Your numbers will differ, and that's exactly the point: generic advice can't answer “can I afford this?” Only your own amortization schedule can.

askZero.heading: Just ask Zero
askZero.p1: There's no form to find and no calculator buried in a menu. Open Zero — the coach lives one tap away anywhere in the app — and type the question the way you'd say it out loud: “can I afford $400 for a winter jacket?” That phrase is the trigger. The moment Zero sees “can I afford” with an amount, Tether-Zero quietly starts a real simulation against your debt payoff plan while Zero reads the rest of your message.
askZero.p2: Two things happen in parallel. Zero talks the decision through with the full context of your finances — that conversation is guidance, not arithmetic. The precise math comes from the simulator, which runs your amortization schedule twice: once as things stand today, and once with the purchase added to your top-priority debt. Same engine, same <link2>payoff strategy</link2> you already committed to — Snowball or Avalanche — and the same promotional rates, if a card is inside a promo window. The difference between those two futures is the honest answer.

readingCard.heading: Reading the Opportunity Cost card
readingCard.p1: A moment later, a card labeled Opportunity Cost appears right in the chat. Its layout is deliberately blunt: “IF YOU SPEND $400” across the top, then the headline — how many days “DEBT FREE PUSHED BACK” — followed by your New Debt Free Date and the Extra interest the purchase would cost. Two facts, zero scolding.
readingCard.p2: Measuring in days is what makes the card land. “$31 of extra interest” is easy to shrug off; “eighteen more days of payments” is not, because time is the thing you're actually trying to buy back. The card converts an invisible balance change into calendar — a unit your gut already understands.

twoButtons.heading: Two honest buttons
twoButtons.p1: Beneath the numbers sit two buttons, and neither one is a guilt trip. “Proceed with purchase” does exactly what it says: the simulation never touched your data, nothing changes in your budget, and Zero simply notes that you chose to go ahead. Sometimes eighteen days is a fair trade for a jacket you'll wear for five winters. The product is clarity, not judgment.
twoButtons.p2: The other button gives deferred gratification real teeth: “Redirect $400 to debt.” Decide the purchase isn't worth it, choose which debt account should receive the money, and Tether-Zero makes it concrete — the amount is applied as a snowflake payment, an extra one-time payment against the balance you picked. The money you almost spent starts pulling your Debt Free Date closer instead of pushing it away.

whenToRun.heading: When to run the numbers
whenToRun.p1: The simulator earns its keep on the purchases households actually argue about. A $2,000 appliance is rarely an impulse buy — it's a negotiation. Instead of trading feelings across the kitchen table, run the simulation and put the card between you: this is what it does to our date. Partners don't have to agree on the purchase, but they'll finally be disagreeing about the same numbers.
whenToRun.p2: For everything else, make it a reflex above a threshold you choose — $100, $200, whatever matches your budget's nerves. The goal was never to stop buying things; it's to stop buying them blind. Some days the answer is “redirect,” and your future self gets the win. Other days the answer is “proceed” — and it may be the most peaceful purchase you make all year, because for once you paid knowing the whole price.

windfallInterceptor.title: What to Do With a Windfall: How Tether-Zero Catches Surprise Money Before It Melts Away

intro.p1: A tax refund lands. A bonus clears. A relative is generous, an old employer sends a final check, an insurance claim finally pays out. Ask that same household two months later what the money did, and the answer is usually a shrug: nothing was squandered on a yacht, yet the balance is gone. Windfalls rarely get stolen — they get absorbed.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero refuses to let that happen quietly. The app watches your synced accounts for deposits that don't look like your normal income, and when one arrives, Zero — the AI coach built into the app — intercepts it with a single question: do you want this money to move your Debt Free Date? This article walks through the Windfall Interceptor: how it spots surprise money, what one tap does with it, and why the decision works best in the moment the money lands.

whyDisappear.heading: Why windfalls disappear
whyDisappear.p1: Behavioral economists call it mental accounting: the same dollar feels different depending on the pocket it arrives in. Salary is serious money, budgeted and spoken for. A windfall arrives with no job assigned — and money without a job drifts toward whatever the month happens to want. A slightly nicer grocery run, one extra dinner out, a purchase that was “almost justified” anyway.
whyDisappear.p2: The window for deciding is short. The day a windfall lands, it still feels like an event — special money, worth a special decision. Give it a week in your checking account and it fades into the balance, indistinguishable from the rest. The fix isn't more discipline; it's timing. You need the question — what is this money for? — to arrive while the money still feels like a windfall.

meetInterceptor.heading: Meet the Windfall Interceptor
meetInterceptor.p1: Tether-Zero automates the timing. When a synced account receives a deposit noticeably larger than your typical income — on the order of 1.2 times your recent average — the app flags it as a pending windfall decision. The next time you open your dashboard, a section called Coach's Corner appears with a card marked “WINDFALL DETECTED”: the deposit amount, how it compares to your average income, and the account it landed in.
meetInterceptor.p2: The card also names where the money could go. Tether-Zero already knows your payoff plan from the Debt Crusher, so the suggestion targets your number-one priority debt under your active strategy — the smallest balance if you run Debt snowball, the most expensive interest rate on Debt avalanche. Underneath sit exactly two buttons: “Apply as Snowflake” and “Not now.”

oneTap.heading: One tap from deposit to debt progress
oneTap.p1: Tap “Apply as Snowflake” and the deposit becomes a snowflake payment — the Debt Crusher's name for extra, unexpected money applied on top of your regular plan. Tether-Zero recalculates your entire payoff schedule on the spot and answers with a confirmation card: “Snowflake applied,” the amount sent, how many days your Debt Free Date just moved, and the new date itself.
oneTap.p2: The card even draws it: a small timeline from today to your new Debt Free Date, with the old date noted beside it. Days are the unit that makes windfalls worth catching. A thousand dollars toward the card is abstract; “debt-free five weeks sooner” is a month of your life handed back — a receipt you can feel, printed in the moment the decision still feels good.

stayInCharge.heading: You stay in charge
stayInCharge.p1: The Interceptor is a prompt, not an automation. No money moves until you tap — Tether-Zero never sweeps a deposit into debt on its own. And “Not now” means never for that deposit: a declined windfall is recorded, the card disappears, and the app will not ask about the same transaction again. One question, one answer, no nagging.
stayInCharge.p2: Household roles are respected too. Only Admins and Editors — the people who can move money in your plan — see the windfall prompt at all. A partner or family member with view-only access can watch the Debt Free Date improve, but the decision stays with the people authorized to make it.

quietUntilNeeded.heading: Quiet until it matters
quietUntilNeeded.p1: Coach's Corner is not another widget competing for attention. The section exists on your dashboard only while a windfall decision is actually pending; answer the question and it folds away. No streaks, no badges, no “insights” manufactured to justify a notification — the Interceptor speaks only when there is genuinely something to decide.
quietUntilNeeded.p2: It also waits until it knows you. Detection needs at least a month of income history and a few income deposits before it starts flagging anything, so a freshly connected account isn't peppered with false alarms while the app learns what normal looks like for your household. The threshold does the same filtering job on the other end: an ordinary paycheck never triggers the card, because ordinary is exactly what it's measured against.

beyondDebt.heading: Not every windfall belongs to debt
beyondDebt.p1: Sometimes “Not now” is the right answer, and the Interceptor treats it as a first-class choice. If your emergency fund is thin, topping it up may beat any interest math. If December, insurance renewals, or a car repair are looming, routing the money into <link>sinking funds</link> converts a surprise deposit into several predictable months. The feature's job isn't to funnel everything into debt — it's to make sure the money gets a deliberate job before it evaporates.
beyondDebt.p2: One boundary worth knowing: a windfall is a surprise, not a pattern. If your income naturally swings — commissions, gig work, seasonal contracts — a big deposit may just be a good month, and the answer is a <link2>budgeting system built for an irregular paycheck</link2> rather than a one-off decision. And when a true windfall does land, splitting it is perfectly legal: a little celebration, the rest toward the date. The plan that survives is the one that leaves room to be human.

aiFinancialCoach.title: Meet Zero, Your AI Money Coach: Real Answers from Your Real Numbers

intro.p1: Budgeting advice is everywhere, and almost all of it is written for nobody in particular. Spend less than you earn. Cook at home. Pay yourself first. None of it can answer the question you actually have on a Tuesday night, which is always specific: is my grocery budget going to survive the month? Should this bonus go to the credit card or the car loan? Can I afford the flight?
intro.p2: Tether-Zero's answer to that gap is Zero, the AI financial coach built into every page of the app. Zero doesn't hand you articles — it reads your real household numbers, answers in plain language, and when action makes sense, it offers one. You'll find its advice specific for the same reason your questions are: it's looking at your budget, not a textbook.

askAnywhere.heading: A coach on every page
askAnywhere.p1: Zero lives behind a small teal button that follows you through the whole dashboard — budget, transactions, goals, Debt Crusher, insights. Hover it and it says exactly what it's for: “Ask Zero.” One tap slides a chat panel in over whatever you're doing, greets you by name, and invites the question: “Ask me anything about your finances.” No context switch, no separate app, no hunting through menus.
askAnywhere.p2: The panel also knows where you are. The suggested prompts that appear match the screen you're on, so from the budget page you'll see budget questions and from Debt Crusher you'll see payoff questions. If you're not sure what to ask, choose Browse prompts to open the Prompt Library — ready-made questions in nine categories, from Budget and Transactions to Debt Crusher and Financial Wellness. Answers stream in like a conversation, and yours picks up where you left it.

realAnswers.heading: Real answers start with your real numbers
realAnswers.p1: Any chatbot can define the avalanche method. Zero is different because it's connected to your actual household data — your categories, balances, debts, and plan. Ask “Am I on track this month?” and the answer comes from how your budget is actually pacing, not from a listicle. Ask “Snowball or avalanche?” and Zero can talk about the trade-off in terms of your balances and rates, the ones it can see.
realAnswers.p2: It gets sharper when money is about to move. Type “can I afford $500” and Zero triggers Tether-Zero's Opportunity Cost simulator, which runs your real payoff plan twice — with and without the purchase — and drops a card into the chat showing your new Debt Free Date and the extra interest the purchase would create. We wrote a whole guide to that one: what does that purchase really cost?

coachsCorner.heading: Coaching you didn't have to ask for
coachsCorner.p1: Zero also speaks up on its own, in the right moments. The dashboard's Coach's Corner is where its observations land. When an unusually large deposit arrives — a bonus, a refund, a windfall — Zero flags it and offers to apply the money as a Snowflake payment toward your priority debt, before it dissolves into everyday spending. (Here's how the windfall play works.)
coachsCorner.p2: The corner watches quieter signals too. A pacing warning tells you a category is on track to run out before the month does — while there's still time to adjust. A No-New-Debt Streak card counts the months since you last opened a new debt account, turning restraint into something you can watch grow. And Subscriptions Worth a Look adds up what your recurring charges really cost per month and per year. Every card can be hidden in Preferences: it's coaching, not nagging.

inControl.heading: You stay in control — always
inControl.p1: Every suggestion Zero makes arrives as an offer with two buttons, never as an action already taken. A windfall card asks Apply as Snowflake or Not now. The opportunity-cost card asks whether to redirect the money to debt or Proceed with purchase — and proceeding is a fine answer; the point is choosing it with open eyes. Nothing in your plan changes without your yes.
inControl.p2: Tether-Zero is also honest about what an AI coach is. Right under the chat box, the app says so in its own words: “Zero uses AI. Verify important financial decisions.” Zero is a coach, not an oracle — fast with your numbers, useful for framing a decision, and worth double-checking when the stakes are high. Your conversation is yours, too: clear it any time from the panel's options menu.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting the most from your coach
gettingStarted.p1: Zero's answers are only as good as the numbers behind them, so the best first move has nothing to do with chat: connect your accounts and keep your budget assigned. A coach reading a current, honest budget gives current, honest answers. From there, let the Prompt Library carry you past the blank-input problem — pick a question that's close to yours and edit it.
gettingStarted.p2: Then make it a rhythm. A one-question check-in — “Am I on track this month?” — takes less than a minute. Ask before big purchases instead of after. And let Coach's Corner do the watching between visits; you bring the questions, it brings the interruptions worth having. That's the whole idea of Zero: not more financial content, just real answers from your real numbers, exactly when you need them.

goalsAndDebt.title: Saving for a Dream While Killing Your Debt: Goals and Debt Without the Guilt

intro.p1: The standard advice for people in debt is monastic: no trips, no upgrades, no dreams until the last balance dies. It reads as discipline and it works — for about three months. Then a friend books the flight you didn't, the plan starts to feel like punishment, and one bad week takes the whole budget down with it. Deprivation isn't a strategy; it's a countdown.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero takes a different position: the dream belongs in the budget, right next to the debt. Financial Goals live alongside the Debt Crusher as first-class citizens — with their own progress bars, their own pace math, and one unusual habit: when a goal and your payoff plan compete for the same dollars, the app doesn't referee your values. It prices the trade-off, in months, and lets you decide. This article shows how that works — and why a number turns out to be so much kinder than guilt.

dreamsAreFuel.heading: Deprivation is not a strategy
dreamsAreFuel.p1: Every all-or-nothing debt plan makes the same bet: that you can want nothing for two years. Real budgets lose that bet constantly, and the loss is expensive — abandoning a payoff plan in month four usually costs more than a modest goal ever would have. A dream does the opposite of what the guilt says it does. It gives the grind a finish line you actually care about, and people who can see the reward keep showing up.
dreamsAreFuel.p2: The real problem was never wanting things. It's not knowing what the wanting costs. When the price of a goal is vague — “this probably slows my debt payoff… somehow… by some amount” — every contribution to it carries a little cloud of guilt, and every debt payment carries a little resentment. The fix isn't to want less. It's to know exactly what the dream costs, in the only currency a payoff plan runs on: time.

honestTradeoff.heading: An honest warning, not a lecture
honestTradeoff.p1: Create a goal in Tether-Zero — the form's own example placeholder suggests “Hawaii vacation” — and give it a target amount and target date. If funding it at the required pace would compete with your payoff plan, the app says so before you commit, in an amber banner: “This goal conflicts with your Debt Crusher plan.” Below it come the specifics: how many dollars a month would be redirected from your debt payoff, and two cards side by side — your current debt-free date next to the projected one, with the delay spelled out plainly, like “Slips by 4 months.”
honestTradeoff.p2: Then comes the sentence that makes the whole feature guilt-free: “You can still create the goal — we'll update your Debt Crusher projection.” No blocking, no scolding, no dark-pattern detour to talk you out of it. If Hawaii is worth four more months of payments, that is a legitimate choice — your <link>payoff strategy</link> keeps running, just with an honest new date. Guilt thrives on vagueness. A trade-off you accepted with open eyes leaves it very little to feed on.

dreamVisible.heading: Make the dream visible
dreamVisible.p1: A goal in Tether-Zero looks like the thing you want, not like a spreadsheet row. Every goal takes a cover image — upload your own or search Unsplash right inside the app — so the beach, the car, or the front porch sits at the top of the page. The Insights dashboard even has a Goal Image Reveal card that uncovers more of the photo as your funded percentage climbs: at 40% funded, you can already see almost half the dream.
dreamVisible.p2: Milestones get celebrated out loud. Cross a quarter and the app cheers “25% Funded!”; reach the middle and it's “Halfway There!”; land the last dollar and a celebration overlay declares “Goal Complete!” It sounds small until you remember the alternative — silence — which is all the old spreadsheet ever offered. Debt payoff has a Debt Free Date to look forward to; now the saving side has fireworks of its own.

stayOnPace.heading: A pace, not a plea
stayOnPace.p1: Behind every goal runs the same time-denominated honesty the Debt Crusher is built on. From your target amount and date, Tether-Zero computes “Required per month” — the contribution that keeps you on schedule — and labels the goal plainly: On track, Ahead, Behind, or At risk. No mystery about whether the dream is drifting; the page tells you before the drift becomes a year.
stayOnPace.p2: The budget does the remembering for you. A “Goals this month” strip sits inside your monthly budget, and one tap on “Fund all at suggested pace” contributes to every active goal at once — with amounts adjusted proportionally to the income you actually have available, so a lean month funds the dream lightly instead of wrecking the plan. Categories linked to a goal carry a small Goal badge, keeping the connection visible right where you allocate.

everySource.heading: Feed it from anywhere
everySource.p1: Contributions come in four flavors: Monthly allocation for the steady drip, One-time transfer for the deliberate move, Linked account when a real savings account backs the goal, and — the fun one — Windfall. The contribution note field suggests its own examples: “tax refund, birthday money, overtime pay.” Tether-Zero already intercepts windfalls for your debt plan; goals are the other honest destination for surprise money, and the app treats them that way.
everySource.p2: Goals belong to the household, not to one login. Every contribution is recorded with the contributor's name, so your partner's fifty dollars toward the trip shows up as theirs, and the goal page keeps a running contributor breakdown. A shared dream with shared receipts survives arguments that a vague joint intention wouldn't. There's even a goal journal for marking the moments — and a retrospective to read back once the dream is funded.

permissionToPause.heading: Permission to pause
permissionToPause.p1: Some months the answer is neither guilt nor grind — it's “not right now.” Tether-Zero lets you pause a goal in two taps: the progress stays, the history stays, the photo stays; contributions simply stop counting against your pace until you resume. Pausing is not quitting, and the app is built to know the difference.
permissionToPause.p2: Priorities drag into a new order when life reorders itself, and a goal you created in January can wait out a rough spring without a single deleted dollar. That is the quiet thesis of the whole feature: a plan survives contact with real life only if wanting things, slowing down, and starting again are all legal moves. Price the trade-offs, celebrate the milestones, pause without penalty — and both dates on that warning card eventually arrive.

connectYourBank.title: Get Your Money Into Tether-Zero: Bank Linking, File Imports, and Auto-Categorization

intro.p1: A budget is a plan for money that actually moves — and it can only steer what it can see. Every method Tether-Zero teaches, from envelope allocations to the Debt Free Date, starts from the same raw material: your real transactions, in the app, categorized. Which makes the first practical question of any new budget refreshingly unglamorous: how does your money get in there?
intro.p2: Tether-Zero gives you three doors. Link your bank and let transactions flow in on their own. Import files when you're bringing history from a bank export or another budgeting app. Or enter transactions by hand whenever that's easiest. Most households end up using a mix, and the app is built so all three land in the same place: one transaction list, one review flow, one budget.

bankLinking.heading: Link your bank, stop typing
bankLinking.p1: The fastest door is the Connect Your Bank page. It walks you through Plaid — the connection service used across the finance industry — to link your institution in a couple of minutes — the page even explains its own pipeline in three words: connect, sync, categorize. The security model is worth spelling out, and the app does, right on the page: your banking credentials are handled by Plaid, never stored by Tether-Zero, and the connection is read-only. Tether-Zero can see transactions and balances; nobody can move your money from inside a budgeting app.
bankLinking.p2: Once linked, new transactions are imported automatically and updated daily, with a Sync all accounts button for the reconciliation nights when you want the freshest data on demand. Everything that arrives this way wears a Linked badge, and its date, amount, and payee are protected — your bank is the source of truth, so those fields can't drift. Two honest notes: bank sync is a premium add-on, and linking is for household Admins and Editors. If you ever disconnect, the account simply becomes a manual one — every transaction you've synced stays.

fileImports.heading: Moving in? Bring your history
fileImports.p1: Switching from another budgeting app, or starting from a pile of bank statement exports? Tap Import on the Transactions page and the Import Transactions wizard takes CSV, OFX, or QFX files up to 5MB and walks three steps: upload the file and pick the destination account, preview the first rows, and review the results. There's no column-mapping puzzle to solve — the columns are detected automatically on the server.
fileImports.p2: The import is built to be hard to regret. Duplicates are detected and skipped automatically, so re-importing an overlapping statement won't double your history. The import only ever adds transactions — it never modifies or deletes what's already there. And the results screen tells you exactly what happened: how many rows imported, how many were skipped, and why, down to the row.

smartMatch.heading: Categorization that learns from you
smartMatch.p1: Getting transactions in is half the job; putting them in the right category is the other half. That's where Smart Match earns its name. When you pick a payee you've used before, a Suggested category chip appears with your usual category for that payee — accept it with one click, or dismiss it and choose another. Either way, you keep the final say.
smartMatch.p2: The clever part is what happens when you override: the rule updates. Categorize your grocery store differently once, and Smart Match learns your correction for next time. The rules are your household's own — built from your history, not everyone else's — and a suggestion only appears when the match is confident (above 80%), so the chip stays helpful instead of noisy — staying silent when it isn't sure is part of the design.

pendingReview.heading: You get the final say
pendingReview.p1: Automation never gets to write your record unsupervised. Transactions that arrive from your bank land in a Pending review state: recognized ones you Accept, unrecognized ones you Reject — with an explicit confirmation, since rejecting deletes the transaction permanently. Both happen inline on the transaction row, and bulk accept exists for the Monday-morning pile.
pendingReview.p2: Accepted transactions can later be marked Cleared as you check them against a statement — the modern version of balancing a checkbook. The result is a register you actually trust: nothing enters your budget without passing under your eyes, and nothing unrecognized gets to sit there polluting your reports.

fromInbox.heading: From inbox to budget
fromInbox.p1: Once the pipes are connected, momentum builds fast. Give the first batch of imported transactions categories — Smart Match makes the second batch faster than the first — and then put the data to work: <link>build your first budget</link> on numbers that are real rather than remembered. That's the difference between budgeting from memory and budgeting from evidence.
fromInbox.p2: From there, the rest of Tether-Zero wakes up. Fresh transactions power the pacing math that <link2>catches overspending early</link2>, feed the insights dashboard, and give Zero, the AI coach, real numbers to answer with. Every one of those features is only as current as your transaction data — which is exactly why getting your money in is step one.

budgetWithPartner.title: Budgeting Is a Team Sport: Running One Budget as a Household

intro.p1: Most money arguments aren't really about money — they're about information. Two people, two banking apps, two mental ledgers, and a monthly reconciliation performed from memory at the kitchen table. When the facts live in different places, every conversation starts with establishing what's true before anyone can discuss what to do about it.
intro.p2: Tether-Zero is built household-first to close exactly that gap. The budget, the accounts, the debts, and the goals don't belong to a login — they belong to the household, and every member sees the same living picture. Same categories, same balances, same progress bars — updated for everyone the moment anything changes. Bring your partner in, and establishing the facts stops being a conversation. It's just the screen you're both looking at.

oneBudget.heading: One budget, both names on it
oneBudget.p1: Share a household and you share everything that matters: the same categories, the same account balances, the same Debt Free Date. When one of you categorizes a transaction or moves money between envelopes, the other sees it — no exporting, no screenshots, no “wait, which number is right?” The app's whole surface, from the budget page to the insights dashboard, reads from the household, not the individual. Goals you fund together, debts you're crushing together, the dashboard you check together — all of it one record.
oneBudget.p2: That changes the texture of money conversations. Instead of comparing recollections, you point at the same chart. Instead of asking your partner what they spent, you both watched the grocery envelope drain in real time. Disagreements don't vanish — but they get to start from shared evidence, which is most of the battle.

roles.heading: Three roles, honest boundaries
roles.p1: Not everyone in a household needs the same keys. Tether-Zero has three roles. An Admin has full control, including inviting and removing members — whoever creates the household starts as its Admin. An Editor can do all the day-to-day work: budget, add accounts, log transactions, manage debts and goals — everything except manage members. A Viewer sees everything and changes nothing.
roles.p2: The Viewer role is quietly the most versatile. It fits the family member who wants visibility without responsibility, the accountability buddy cheering on your payoff, even a financial coach you've asked to look over your plan. And the boundaries are enforced, not implied: the invite dialog states each role's access in plain terms, and the app holds to it everywhere — including Zero, the AI coach, which tailors what it offers to what your role can actually do.

inviting.heading: The invite takes a minute
inviting.p1: Adding your partner is a settings-page errand, not a project. Open Settings → Household → Members, choose Invite Member, enter their email, and pick their role. The dialog spells out what each role can do right where you choose it, so nobody is guessing what they're handing over. They get an email with a secure link; clicking it lands on an accept page that works whether they already have a Tether-Zero account or are creating one on the spot.
inviting.p2: The mechanics are built for real life. Each invite link is single-use and expires after 72 hours — so a stale email sitting in an inbox isn't a standing security hole — and you can resend or revoke a pending invitation any time. Households hold up to five members, and the Members page shows the capacity right on the screen, so there's no guessing.

changeAndLeave.heading: People change; the budget survives
changeAndLeave.p1: Roles aren't tattoos. An Admin can change any member's role from the same Members page — promote your partner to Admin, move a coach from Editor down to Viewer when the engagement ends. Removing a member revokes their access immediately, but deletes nothing: the household's budget, accounts, and history stay exactly as they were.
changeAndLeave.p2: Leaving works the same way in reverse — walk away, and the household continues for everyone else. The one guardrail: the last Admin can't leave without first promoting someone, so a household is never orphaned. It's the same principle throughout: access should match your life today, and changing it should never put the shared record at risk.

teamPlays.heading: Plays for the two-player game
teamPlays.p1: The setup takes minutes; the payoff comes from how you use it. The play that matters most is the weekly check-in: ten minutes, same screen, walking the budget together. If you're both Editors, categorize your own spending as it happens — Smart Match learns from each of you, and nobody inherits the other person's backlog. And when a decision is bigger than an envelope, <link2>ask Zero together</link2> — the coach answers from your shared numbers.
teamPlays.p2: If you're just starting, do the first build as a pair: <link>set up your first budget</link> with both of you in the room, because the person who helps assign the dollars is the person who defends the plan later. One budget, two sets of eyes, no competing versions of the truth. That's the team sport — and it's a lot more fun to win together.
