meta.title: What Did the Vacation Actually Cost?
meta.description: Vacation spending scatters across categories. Tether-Zero's tags collect it — and Zero totals it — so one question finally has one answer.

spendingTags.title: Beyond Categories: Answer “What Did the Vacation Actually Cost?” with Tags

intro.p1: The vacation was one decision. The budget remembers it as five: a bigger grocery week, two tanks of gas, a hotel under Travel, restaurants that blurred into your normal dining out, and an airport coffee that vanished into Miscellaneous. Ask your budget “what did the trip cost?” and it shrugs — every dollar is accounted for, and the answer is still nowhere.
intro.p2: That's not a flaw in your categories; it's their design. Categories are built to answer a monthly question — where does the money go? — one label per line, the same shape every month. Some questions run sideways across that structure. For those, Tether-Zero has a second axis: tags. This article shows how a two-minute label turns “roughly a lot” into an actual number — for vacations, remodels, tax season, and any other project your money touches.

whyCategoriesFail.heading: Why categories can't answer it
whyCategoriesFail.p1: Categories are the load-bearing walls of a zero-based budget: exclusive, monthly, one per transaction line. That rigidity is a feature — it's what makes “every dollar has a job” checkable. But an event like a vacation is cross-cutting by nature. Its spending lands in groceries, gas, dining, and lodging, and it should stay there: those categories still need honest monthly totals.
whyCategoriesFail.p2: The tempting workaround — a “Vacation” category — quietly breaks both answers. Move the trip's groceries out of Groceries and your grocery history lies; leave them in and your vacation total lies. The real fix isn't a better category. It's a second, independent label that rides along wherever the spending happens — which is exactly what the app's own tour says tags are for: “Tags cut across categories, so you can track things like a vacation or a project wherever the spending happens.”

meetTags.heading: Meet the Tags page
meetTags.p1: Tags live on their own page in the sidebar, and they belong to the household — create “Hawaii 2026” once and everyone's transactions can wear it. A tag is deliberately simple: a name up to 50 characters and, if you like, one of twelve preset colors so it stands out in lists. The list stays alphabetical, so a consistent naming habit (“Trip: Hawaii”, “Trip: Thanksgiving”) keeps related tags together.
meetTags.p2: Two practical notes. Names are case-sensitive — “vacation” and “Vacation” are two different tags, as the app's own tour warns — so pick a capitalization and stick with it. And roles matter: everyone in the household can see the tags, Editors can create and edit them, and only Admins can delete one. A label your whole household reports against deserves that small amount of governance.

tagAsYouGo.heading: Tag it while it's fresh
tagAsYouGo.p1: Tagging works best as a habit of the moment, and the transaction form is built for that. Every transaction takes tags from a multi-select — “Select tags” — and a single purchase can wear several at once: the resort dinner can be “Hawaii 2026” and “Anniversary” simultaneously, something no category could ever allow.
tagAsYouGo.p2: Mid-entry, if the tag doesn't exist yet, you don't leave the form: a “+ Create new tag” option sits right in the picker. Standing in the rental-car line is exactly when “Hawaii 2026” should be born — because the alternative is a month-end archaeology dig through statements, reconstructing which of forty grocery lines were the trip.

splitTheReceipt.heading: Split the receipt, keep the truth
splitTheReceipt.p1: Real receipts are rarely pure. The big-box run before the trip was a cooler, sunscreen, and beach towels — plus a normal week of groceries. Tag the whole transaction “Hawaii 2026” and your vacation total inflates; skip it and the trip looks cheaper than it was. Tether-Zero's answer is the split: divide the transaction into lines, and each line carries its own category and its own optional tag.
splitTheReceipt.p2: So the cooler and sunscreen go on a “Hawaii 2026” line and the regular groceries stay untagged, with the split editor checking that the lines add up to the original amount. The vacation number stays honest to the dollar, and nobody invents fake transactions to get there.

askZeroForTheBill.heading: Ask Zero for the bill
askZeroForTheBill.p1: When the trip is over, the transactions list shows you the story: filter by tag — the filter's placeholder reads “Any tag” — and every “Hawaii 2026” line from every category stands in one place. That's the browsing half. For the arithmetic, ask <link>Zero</link>, the AI coach built into the app, as plainly as you like: what did everything tagged Hawaii 2026 cost?
askZeroForTheBill.p2: Totals by tag are squarely inside Zero's job description — the app's own prompt library seeds questions like “What's my total spending across all transactions tagged as Medical this year so far?” and comparing two months of spending filtered to a single “Date Night” tag. Your vacation question is the same sentence with your tag in it. One label while you spend; one question when you're done.

oneLabelManyJobs.heading: One label, many jobs
oneLabelManyJobs.p1: Vacation is just the gateway use. The same mechanism runs an expense report — tag work costs “Reimbursable” and pull the list before submitting. It survives tax season, where a “Tax Deductible” tag collects the audit trail all year. It keeps a remodel honest, because “Home Renovation” doesn't care whether the money left through the hardware store or a plumber's invoice. And Zero will even help you design a tagging strategy if you tell it how your finances are shaped.
oneLabelManyJobs.p2: When a tag starts measuring something you're still saving for, the two systems meet: the prompt library's own example asks whether a Vacation tag and a separate vacation goal should coexist. They can — they face opposite directions. A <link2>goal funds the dream</link2> before you leave; a tag measures what it actually cost once you're back. Run both, and the next trip gets planned with real numbers instead of a wince.

moneyStory.title: Reading Your Money Story: Net Worth, Age of Money, and Your Income-vs-Expenses Trend

intro.p1: A budget is very good at this month. It hands every dollar a job, warns you when a category runs hot, and gets you to the next payday with a plan. What it's quieter about is the part that matters most over years: whether the months are adding up to anything. Am I better off than I was in March? Is the paycheck-to-paycheck feeling actually fading, or does it just have better paperwork now?
intro.p2: Those are story questions, and stories need more than one frame. Tether-Zero's Insights dashboard is where your transactions stop being a list and start being a plot: a grid of cards, each tracking one number in motion. This article reads the three that carry the main storyline — Net Worth, Age of Money, and Income vs. Expense — and shows how they answer, month by month, the only question that outlasts every budget cycle: is this working?

whereTheStoryLives.heading: Where the story lives
whereTheStoryLives.p1: Open Insights from the sidebar and you land on the Financial tab — a grid of cards, each one a chapter. The time machine sits at the top: a date-range selector that runs from This Month and Last Month through Last 3 Months, Year to Date, and Last Year, plus a custom range for when you want to inspect exactly the stretch a job change or a move carved out.
whereTheStoryLives.p2: None of the cards is a dead end. Click one and it opens into a detail view with the underlying transactions — so when a number surprises you, the receipts that produced it are one tap away. A story you can audit is a story you can trust.

netWorthChapter.heading: Net worth: the wide-angle shot
netWorthChapter.p1: Net worth is the bluntest number you own: everything you have minus everything you owe. Tether-Zero computes it straight from your accounts — cash and savings on one side, credit cards and loans on the other — and shows the current figure with its change since the start of your selected range, alongside a line tracing the trajectory week by week, or month by month on longer ranges.
netWorthChapter.p2: Here's the quietly humane part: the chart is built for people who start below zero. A visible zero line crosses the graph, the stretch beneath it draws in red and the stretch above in green — because for a household mid-payoff, the story isn't “rich or not.” It's a line climbing toward zero and then through it, and watching that climb is the entire point of the wide-angle shot.

ageOfMoneyChapter.heading: Age of money: the tempo
ageOfMoneyChapter.p1: Age of Money answers a stranger, sharper question: when you spend a dollar today, how long ago did you earn it? The card matches each expense to the income that funded it — oldest income first — and reports the average gap in days. Ten days means you're spending money that landed a week and a half ago; forty means today's groceries were paid for by a paycheck from early last month. In the app's own words, it tells you whether you're spending last week's income or last month's.
ageOfMoneyChapter.p2: Higher is better — older money means a deeper cushion between earning and needing. The number grows slowly, which is honest: breathing room is built, not toggled. Two footnotes worth knowing: the card needs cleared transactions to do its matching, and the display caps at “365+” — past a full year of cushion, the app considers the point made.

incomeVsExpenseChapter.heading: Income vs. expense: the engine
incomeVsExpenseChapter.p1: The third card is the simplest and the most consequential: for each month in your range, two bars — what came in, what went out. The gap between them is the engine of everything else in Tether-Zero. It's the money that becomes debt payments, goal contributions, and an aging Age of Money; when the bars touch, or cross, the other charts stall with them.
incomeVsExpenseChapter.p2: The card's real gift is trend-sight. A single tight month reads as an emergency when it's actually just December; three shrinking gaps in a row read as fine when they're actually a drift. Laid out by month, noise and plot separate on their own — and you respond to the plot, not the noise.

readingItTogether.heading: Reading the chapters together
readingItTogether.p1: The three cards are one story told at three speeds. The income-expense gap is the fastest signal — it moves the month it happens. Age of Money is the medium one: sustain a gap and the average slowly climbs as newer spending draws on older income. Net worth is the slow arc that compounds the other two, quarter after quarter. When all three lean the same way, you don't have to wonder whether things are working; when they disagree, the disagreement itself tells you where to look.
readingItTogether.p2: The date ranges are your zoom lens. This Month answers “how's it going?”; Year to Date answers “what kind of year is this?”; Last Year, read once, is the closest thing a budget offers to rereading an old journal. Same numbers, different altitude — pick the one that matches the question you're actually asking.

fromStoryToNextChapter.heading: From story to next chapter
fromStoryToNextChapter.p1: The dashboard bends to what you care about. A customize panel lets you choose which cards show, and there are more chapters waiting when you want them: Top Payees for “where does it all actually go?”, a Pacing Gauge for the current month's speed, and a whole Freedom tab where your debt payoff draws its burndown. The Goals tab keeps your dreams' progress — photo reveal included — in the same reading room.
fromStoryToNextChapter.p2: And when a trend needs interpreting rather than admiring, the reader-in-residence is <link>Zero</link>: ask why net worth dipped in March or what would push Age of Money past thirty, and the answer comes grounded in your actual transactions. Day to day, <link2>Spending Pace</link2> still guards the current month — Insights is where you step back and read the arc those months are writing.
